symptom: In a disposable Linux synthetic probe, closing a previously correct final-directory FD and retaining only its integer allowed a later unrelated directory open to reuse that integer. RENAME_NOREPLACE using the stale integer published the decoy JSON, not the originally authorized JSON. Keeping a live dup of the original FD instead published the original and left the decoy staged bytes unchanged. This is a candidate-design counterexample, not a production incident.
lesson: A numeric file descriptor is only a process-local index while its kernel handle remains open. Once closed, the same number may refer to a different directory; using it as a stored publisher capability can redirect an otherwise atomic no-replace publication. A live dup retains the original directory object in this bounded fixture but does not authenticate how that object was bootstrapped or guarantee pathname reachability.
guardrail: Do not cache or hand off bare numeric directory FD values beyond their live ownership lifetime. Keep a live owned FD (or explicitly managed dup) throughout each FD-relative publish/read transaction, check its identity and ownership under a separately reviewed bootstrap, and fail closed on lost ownership. Reuse existing parent-swap, openat2 and reachability guardrails; do not treat dup or st_dev/st_ino as independent authority, introduce automatic recovery or deletion, connect Current BUY/LINE/public/production, activate protected N2, or claim power-loss durability.
